XVI.      COMMITTED LIABILITY
16.1       The issue of Committed Liability has been engaging the attention of the Committee since 1997-98.  At the end
of the Eight Five Year Plan, the Planning Commission had issued very detailed guidelines to carry forward the
Committed Expenditure from Plan to the non-plan side.  A lump sum provision of Rs. 500 crores in the Ministry of
Finance Budget for 1997-98 was provided for this purpose.  As a result of this exercise, however, only a sum of Rs.150
crores was transferred from plan to non-plan for the various Ministries as committed expenditure during 1997-98.  Rest
of the amount was surrendered as the proposals were not found acceptable.  The Secretary (Expenditure) while deposing
before the Committee on 27
th March, 1999 had informed that the Tenth Finance Commission had given a breathing time
till 1999-2000 for this transition.
16.2     The Department has now informed that it has reviewed the position regarding transfer of committed liabilities of
the Eighth Plan to the non-plan side. It has been noted that unlike other Ministries and Departments, the programmes
and activities of the  Department of Culture are continuous in nature and most of the plan schemes of the Eighth Plan
can be carried forward to the Ninth Plan.  (without many committed liabilities). 
16.3     The Committee notes with serious concern that while grants for Plan Schemes are getting reduced, non-plan
allocation and expenditure are steadily increasing.  What is happening is that the committed expenditure which should
appropriately be charged to the Pool, is being passed on to the respective Departments which is totally against the
guidelines of Tenth Finance Commission/Planning Commission.  If the committed expenditure is charged to the Pool, it
will not have any burden on the specific schemes of the Department.  Secretary (Expenditure), who appeared before the
Committee last year, was in full agreement  with the stand taken by the Committee.  The Committee is, however,
constrained to observe that in spite of Committee’s repeated efforts/directives to assist the Departments, no progress has
been made in the matter.  It seems that breathing time till 1999-2000 given by the Tenth Finance Commission has not
been availed of by any Department.  There is total lack of initiative on the part of the Departments.  The Committee
again  emphasises that the Department should get this matter resolved without any further delay.  The way the
Department including Ministry of Finance is trying to escape their responsibility is against the expressed wishes of the
Finance Commission and the recommendations made by the Committee.  This tendency, the Committee is constrained
to observe, is not in consonance with the principles which are well-established.  The Committee again reiterates that the
Department should pursue the matter and report to the Committee about the outcome thereof.
XVII.   GENERAL
The Committee notes with concern that some Departments are not furnishing the required information/papers
and Hindi version thereof sought by the Committee on time and sometimes the papers are not even properly arranged
and indexed.  This results in a lot of inconvenience to the Committee.  In such a situation the Members either get very
little time or no time at all to go through the papers and actively participate in the deliberations of the Committee. The
Committee, is therefore, constrained to observe that the communications sent to the Ministries or the Departments by
the Secretariat on behalf of the Committee should be given due attention and all efforts should be made to furnish the
requisite information/ paper to the Committee expeditiously  and within the time limit.

The matter of shortage of Monument Attendants for 3598 Centrally Protected Monuments in the country has
been engaging the attention of the Committee for the last two-three years.  The Committee regrets that the matter has
not yet been sorted out and is still lingering on.  As per the latest information submitted by the Department, it has been
advised by the Planning Commission to identify the monuments for de- protection and transfer them to the State
Archaeology Departments for maintenace in order to reduce its liability.  This suggestion has, however, not been
accepted by the ASI as it constitutes a major policy decision.  Instead a proposal has now been sent by the ASI to the
Planning Commission to create 1564 posts of Monument Attendants for regularising the temporary status of daily
wagers who have been working on the monuments for more than a decade.  In reply to a query as to what is the
experience of the ASI with regard to availability of funds with the State Archaeology Departments, the Committee was
informed that the State Departments of Archaeology are adversely affected because of inadequate allocation of funds. 
In case it is so, the suggestion for de-protection and transfer of the national monuments to State Archaeology
Departments seems to be absurd as the situation will then be worse.  (Para 3.4)
            The Committee would also like to point out that the original requirement of Monument Attendants as projected
by the Department was 5000.   The latest proposal for creation of 1564 posts of Monument Attendants is meant for
regularising the temporary status of daily wagers.  Approval of this proposal by the Planning Commission would not
result in any increase in the existing strength of Monument Attendants.  The Committee is of the view that the stand of
the Planning Commission would indirectly result in further deterioration of the Monuments.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Planning Commission should adopt a positive attitude in the matter in order to preserve our
national heritage. (Para 3.5)

The Committee, is therefore, constrained to observe that the communications sent to the Ministries or the
Departments by the Secretariat on behalf of the Committee should be given due attention and all efforts should be made
to furnish the requisite information/ paper to the Committee expeditiously  and within the time limit.

PREFACE
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this 
Ninety Third Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No.50) of the Department of Elementary
Education and Literacy,  Ministry of Human Resource Development for the year 2000-2001.
2.         The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the Department of
Elementary Education and Literacy, Ministry of Human Resource Development and also heard the Secretary and other
Officials of that Department  on the said Demands for Grants in its meeting held on 23rd & 29th    March, 2000.
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on 13th  April, 2000.
 
 
NEW DELHI;                                                                                                                  S.B.CHAVAN
April  13, 2000             
                                                                                                            Chairman,
Chaitra   24, 1922 (Saka)                                                                     Department related Parliamentary
                                                                                                                          Standing Committee on
                                                                                                                 Human Resource Development
 
REPORT
 
I.          INTRODUCTION
1.1       The  National Policies of Education in India have always underscored the Constitutional resolve to provide
quality education to all.  Hence, to focus on the urgency of universalisation of elementary education, a separate
Department of Elementary Education and Literacy has been created. Education is the key to all processes of
development, especially human development.  Having regard to the size of the population, diversity and economic
frailty prevailing in the country, the challenges in the path of providing Education for All are too many and enormous. 
Education being in the Concurrent List of the Constitution, its meaningful development implies an effective partnership
between the Union Government  and the States.
1.2       The Ninth Plan treats education as the most crucial investment in human development.  Approach Paper to the
Ninth Plan had indicated that `apart from carrying out the direction given by the National Policy of Education 1986 and
Programme of Action, 1992, making the nation fully literate by the year 2005 would be a committed goal.  However,
under the revised scheme of the National Literacy Mission it has been upheld by the literacy experts that full literacy for
India means a sustainable threshold level of 75% and the basic objective should be to seek to achieve high success rates
rather than `total literacy’.  Hence, there is a need that priorities should include universalisation of elementary education,
raising the quality of education at all levels, upliftment of the educational status of disadvantaged groups like
SCs/STs/girls/disabled, equality and removal of regional imbalances, vocationalisation of education and setting up of
centres of excellence.
1.3       During the course of his evidence, the Secretary, Department of Elementary Education and Literacy informed
the Committee that an allocation of Rs. 24,908 crore has been made in the Ninth Five Year Plan in the Central Sector as
against an outlay of Rs. 7,443 crore in the Eighth Five Year Plan. While this represents an increase of more than two
and a half times, it is less than one third of the actual requirement projected.   In view of an anticipated expenditure of
Rs. 11,951,03 crore in the Ninth Plan, an amount of Rs. 12,957.35 crore is expected to be available for allocation 
during the last two years of the current Five Year Plan.  Thus, 50% of the amount i.e. Rs. 6,478.67 crore should have
been allocated to the Department during 2000-2001.  However, actual allocation has been restricted to Rs. 5,450 crore, a
shortfall of approximately, Rs. 1,000 crore, the Secretary clarified.  Allocation for Elementary  Education is   Rs.
3,608.75 crore as against Rs. 3,035.13 crore in 1999-2000 (BE) which shows an increase of 18.9%.  Allocation for
Elementary Education is 66% of total allocation for Central Plan on Education in 2000-2001 as against about 65% last
year.  The Committee was informed  that although several Committees had suggested to increase  allocation for
Education to  6% of GDP, yet,  the present allocation is only 3.4% of GDP which is still less by 2.6%.  The

93RD REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/93rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:11]
Governments’ efforts are to gradually increase the level to 6% of GDP.  The Committee in this respect is of the
considered view that when there is a general trend for disinvestment  of the  public sector and cuts in subsidies, it should
be the effort of the Government to prioritize the Social Sector, especially Education and Health, which stand as the heart
and soul of human development .  The Committee, therefore, suggests that the Department should find ways and means
for further development and promotion of education.
II.         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       The total allocation in BE 1999-2000 for Elementary Education and Literacy was Rs. 3150.37 crore which was
reduced to Rs. 2936.88 crore at the RE stage.  However, there is a  substantive increase of around Rs. 800 crore in 2000-
2001.  The Committee was informed  that allocation of Rs. 3036.95 crore in BE 1999-2000 was reduced to Rs. 2854.24
crore at RE stage as the Schemes for Teacher Education and Non-Formal Education could not be implemented with 
revised norms.  Similarly, the new scheme of National Programme for Women Education could not be launched for
which Rs. 160 crore was provided.  In addition, States and UTs are yet to appoint a sizeable number of teachers
sanctioned under the ‘Operation Blackboard’ due to various reasons.
2.2       During the year 2000-2001, it is proposed to implement  the new Scheme of ‘Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan’ for which
Rs. 350 crore has been allocated.  Similarly, the National Programme for Women Education is also expected to be
launched during the year for which an allocation of Rs.160 crore has been made.  Besides, it is proposed to  implement
the revised schemes of Non-Formal Education and Teacher Education with its enhanced cost  parameters for which an
allocation of Rs. 300 crore and Rs. 219.53 crore respectively has been made.  Hence, the provision in BE 2000-2001 for
the Schemes in Elementary Education Sector has been increased to Rs. 3610.75 crore, the Committee was informed.
2.3       The Committee notes with serious concern that the main reason for reduction of allocation at RE 1999-2000 is
the absence of approval to the expansion, revised and enhanced norms in respect of some of the schemes of elementary
education.  The Committee observes that against the reduced allocation of RE 1999-2000, the reported expenditure upto
29.2.2000 is Rs. 2323.92 crore only.  Therefore, the Committee suggests  that adequate  measures need to be taken for
effective and proper implementation of the schemes of elementary education in  2000-2001.
2.4       Performance Budget should clearly reflect both the financial provision and corresponding physical achievements
of different schemes/programmes during the financial year.  The Committee, however, observes that Performance
Budgets of almost all the Departments are prepared in such a manner that one does not get a clear  idea in this regard. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take corrective steps in this regard, if the
Performance Budgeting is to have any meaning.
III.       LITERACY
3.1       The Committee  was informed that as a result of concerted efforts in the area of primary education, non-formal
education and adult education, there has been some increase in the literacy rate prevailing in the country.  Results of the
53
rd round of the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO) indicate that against the literacy rate of 52.2% in 1991,
this rate was 62% at the end of December, 1997 and is projected to touch 64% at the end of 1998.  This increase of
almost 2% may be seen  against the backdrop of an average decadal growth of only 8.5% between 1951 and 1991. 
Keeping the growth of around 2% per annum, it has been expected that by the year 2005 we could reach a target of 75%
literacy.  Therefore, the revised scheme of National Literacy Mission has put it at a practical level of 75% by 2005.
3.2       Male literacy rates have risen from 64.1% in 1991 to 73% in 1997 and the female literacy rates in the
corresponding period have risen from  39.3% to 50%.  Thus,  the gender gap in literacy rates is being narrowed in
overall terms.  Another encouraging trend is acceleration of literacy rates in rural areas.  While in 1991, the urban
literacy rate was 73.1% and rural literacy rate was 44.7%,  in 1997, as per the  NSSO Survey, urban  literacy rate was 
80% and the rural literacy rate was 56%.    In terms of performance in literacy, Mizoram leads the country with a
literacy rate of 95%.  Kerala now occupies the second place with a literacy rate of 93%.   Almost all the educationally
backward States have also shown reasonable improvement.
3.3       The Committee is inclined to believe that literacy/enrolment/Drop-out rates projected on the basis of surveys
conducted so far do not seem to be realistic.  There is a lot of difference  between assessment made by the grass root
level workers and the so called independent surveys.  The  Committee views with serious concern the difference
between male and female literacy in some of the States as indicated below:

As per the figures available with the Committee based on Census 1991, many districts in Bihar, MP, Rajasthan and UP
had female literacy rate below 20.  The Committee is of the view that sustained efforts should be made by the
Department to bring out improvement in such weak areas.
IV.       UNIVERSALISATION OF ELEMENTARY EDUCATION (UEE)
4.1       The Ninth Plan envisaged Universalisation of Elementary Education to mean universalisation of access,
retention and achievement.   Significant strides in this direction have been made.  The Secretary informed that 94% of
the rural population living in 8.26 lakh habitations has now a school within a walking distance of one km. And 84% of
this population has now an upper primary school within a walking distance of 3 kms.  It was further informed to the
Committee that the revised target for achieving UEE puts emphasis on that - every child in 6-14 age group is either in
school, Education Guarantee Scheme centre or  back to school camp by 2003, five years of primary schooling for every
child by 2007 and eight years of elementary schooling by 2010. 
4.2       The Committee was also given to understand that the revised 83
rd Constitution Amendment Bill, 1997 to make
education for Children from 6-14 years of age a Fundamental Right has been referred to a group of Ministers for
detailed examination of financial and legal aspects and Central legislation for making elementary education free and
compulsory is under consideration. The Committee takes note of the efforts and hopes that the revised target of UEE
would be achieved as per the proposed plan and steps would also be taken to make elementary education free and
compulsory for children of  6-14 age group.
4.3       It has been taken note of by the Committee that the Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) in the primary stage (Class 1-
V) increased from 42.6 percent in 1950-51 to 92.14 % in 1998-99 and in the upper primary stage (class VI-VIII) from
12.7 % to 57.58 % over the same period. However, the Committee observes that gender disparities are conspicuous in
regard to enrolment and retention.   Girls still account for only 43.5% of enrolment at primary stage and 40.5% at upper
primary stage.  The Committee is constrained to note that Uttar Pradesh has the lowest enrolment ratio (49.31) in class
I-V for girls in the country.   So far as upper primary stage is concerned, Bihar and UP have the lowest enrolment ratio
for girls i.e. 23.13 and 26.41 respectively.  The Committee finds that gender disparities are equally evident  so far as
dropout rates are concerned. Dropout rates in classes 1-V for the year 1998-99 (provisional) for boys are  38.62% and
for girls 41.22% and in classes I-VIII   of the same year (provisional) stand for boys 54.40 % and girls 60.09%.  Here
again, states like Bihar, UP, Rajasthan and some NE states are a cause  for concern. 
4.4       Expressing its concern in this regard, the Committee last year had opined that concerted efforts in a mission
mode by all the implementing agencies were required to be made without any delay.   The Committee has been
informed that the State Education Ministers’ Conference held in October., 1998 had recommended that universal
primary education should be pursued in a mission mode .   Subsequently, on the basis of recommendations made by a
National Committee of State Education Ministers, the scheme of ‘Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan’ was evolved.
4.5       The Committee has been informed  that the basic idea is to incorporate existing programmes of elementary
education in the Central and Centrally Sponsored Category under the new scheme in consultation and partnership with
states.
The following goals have been set for the SSA :-
-           all 6-14 age children in school/EGS centre/bridge course by 2003;
-           all 6-14 age children complete 5 years primary education by 2007;and
-           all 6-14 age children complete 8 years of school by 2010.

The approach is community-owned and village education plans prepared in consultation with Panchayati Raj
Institutions, which forms the basis of district primary education plans.   There will be a focus on districts  having low
female literacy among Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The funds under the SSA could be available to the states
on a 85:15 sharing basis for the remaining period of the Ninth Plan.
4.6       The Committee notes that the scheme is under the consideration of the EFC and is likely to be operationalised
soon.   A provision of Rs. 350 crore has been made for it for 2000-2001.   However, the Committee is constrained to
note that allocation for this proposed scheme is being made from 1997-98 onwards .  Rs. 5.00 crore were provided in
BE 1997-98 which was reduced to Rs. 2 lakhs at the RE stage.  Allocation of Rs. 5.00 crore in BE 1998-99 was reduced
to Rs. 1.00 crore at the RE stage.   Rs.10.00 crore were allocated in BE 1999-2000 which was reduced to Rs. 2.00 crore
at the RE stage.
4.7       The Committee feels that three years’  time is unduly long for sanctioning of a scheme.  The Committee,
therefore, desires that all the formalities for approval of this scheme should be completed at the earliest so that it can be
implemented without any further delay.   The Committee is of the view that although the scheme appears to be sound as
it is based on holistic and convergent approach and  integrates the various elementary educational schemes, its success
depends upon its  effective  implementation and monitoring.  Unless the scheme is properly and closely monitored  and
gets the cooperation of all concerned agencies, it may have the fate like many other central schemes and programmes. 
V.        OPERATION BLACK BOARD
5.1       Launched in 1987-88, this programme aims at improving classroom environment by providing infrastructural 
facilities, additional teachers and teaching learning material to primary schools.  It has been extended to upper primary
schools in Eighth Plan.
5.2       The Committee notes that allocation of Rs. 400 crore made for 1999-2000 had to be reduced to Rs. 300 crore at
the RE stage.  Expenditure reported upto 29.2.2000 is Rs. 281.48 crore.  Under-utilisation of funds has been noticed by
the Committee in earlier years  also.   The Committee has been given to understand that most of the states were reluctant
to create additional posts of teachers. Not only this, against 83,045 posts sanctioned for third teacher in primary schools,
74,463 teachers have been appointed by the states.  Position in respect of the following states is a cause of concern :-

appointed so far.  Position in respect of the following states is worth-noting –

5.3       The Committee is perturbed to note that no allocation  was made for Teaching Learning Equipment (TLE)  and
salary of teachers during 1998-99 and 1999-2000 for many states/UTs, such as Bihar, J & K, Kerala, Manipur, A&N
Islands, Chandigarh, D& N Haveli, Daman & Diu & Lakshadweep.   Moreover, A&N Islands could only utilise
40.18%   of the entire fund allocation for the scheme from 1987-88 to 1999-2000.  It was further brought to the notice of
the Committee that no fund was released under Jawahar Rojgar Yojana (JRY) for partly financing the construction of
Primary school Buildings /Rooms under the Scheme to several States such as Goa, M.P., J&K, Maharashtra,
Meghalaya, Tripura, U.P., W.Bengal and  Pondicherry over the last five years.
5.4       The Committee observes that lack of initiative on the part of many  states,  has resulted in unspent balances lying
with them.  As on 10.3.2000, out of Rs. 2590.16 crore released under ‘Operation Blackboard’, an amount of Rs. 378.69

crore is lying unutilised with different state govts.   Bihar, MP and  Orissa have unspent balances of Rs. 51.47 crore, Rs.
48.67 crore and Rs. 46.92 crore respectively.   This calls for serious review of the scheme.   The Committee is of the
view that such a situation is against all budgetary/accounting norms.   Drastic measures need to be taken in this regard.  
The Committee has been informed that a recommendation has been made to the Finance Commission to provide non-
Plan financial assistance to the states to cover  Teachers’ salary.  Instructions have also been issued to States/UTs for
decentralised purchase of Teaching Learning equipment.  The Committee would like to be apprised about the latest
position in this regard.
5.5       The Committee understands that teachers appointed in far flung areas and tribal areas generally avoid going
there.  Because of this, children in those areas suffer.  The Committee feels that the Department needs to give a serious
thought to it to overcome this problem.   One way to address this problem is when the posts are advertised, the place of
posting could be made clear therein.   The Committee would like that the Department may prepare suitable
guidelines/plan of action in this regard and apprise the Committee about it.   The Committee, also, recommends that
there should be a proper monitoring of the schemes pertaining to appointment of teachers, construction of school
buildings and providing TLE to schools.  Periodical  field visits and random inspections without prior intimation to get
first hand information of the scheme should also be undertaken.
5.6       On the question of evaluation of the scheme, the Department informed that an evaluation of the scheme covering
all States had been entrusted to the National Institute of Educational Planning and Administration (NIEPA) during
1997-98.   The final evaluation report is awaited.  The Committee is of the view that NIEPA’s  Report should be
expedited for suitable remedial measures. 
VI.       TEACHERS’ TRAINING PROGRAMME
6.1       Restructuring and Re-organisation of Teacher Education was  launched in 1987 to create a viable institutional
infrastructure, academic and technical resource base for orientation, training and continuous  upgradation of knowledge,
competence and pedagogical skills of elementary school teachers in the country.
6.2       The  Committee was informed that the budgetary allocation for Teachers’ Training Programme was enhanced to
Rs. 290 crore in 1999-2000 as compared to Rs. 159 crore in 1998-99 anticipating revision of norms under the
Programme and the demands from the states for new projects.    The Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) in its
meeting held on 19
th April, 1999 approved the revised norms.   However, for the new projects of DIETs/CTE, EFC felt
that priority should be given to consolidation and operationalistion of the already sanctioned projects and the new
projects should be sanctioned only in those areas which have shown satisfactory performance in this regard.   The
Department has informed that in view of the dissolution of the 12 th Lok Sabha, it was decided that the matter be
processed further for obtaining the approval of the Cabinet only after formation of the new Government.   Accordingly,
the  matter has now been processed in consultation with the Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission and the
proposal of revision of norms is presently before the Cabinet.  In view of the non-revision of norms due to the above
mentioned circumstances, it was felt that it may not be possible to implement the revised norms during the current
financial year.   Accordingly, the budget provision for Teachers’ Training Programme was reduced from Rs. 219 crore
at BE stage to Rs. 150 crore at RE stage.   An expenditure of Rs. 142 crore has already been incurred on continuation
and consolidation of Teachers’ Training Programme  during 1999-2000.  Though, there are proposals from the  state
govts. for opening up 57 new DIETs and 11 CTEs/IASEs, the new projects will be sanctioned only during 2000-2001
after the revised norms are implemented.  Preference will be given to those states who have already operationalised their
sanctioned projects.   The Committee hopes that the new norms will be approved and implemented without further loss
of time and the allocation made in 2000-2001 for this Programme will be fully and properly utilised.
6.3       The main objectives of the National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE), established in 1995, are to achieve
planned and coordinated development of the teacher education system, regulation and proper maintenance of norms and
standards of teacher education.   The Committee observes that due to unspent balances lying with NCTE, allocation of
funds had to be reduced at RE stage in 1997-98 and 1998-99.   An unspent balance of Rs. 0.74 crore was allowed to be
carried forward for utilisation during 1997-98.   During 1998-99, an unspent balance of Rs. 2.02 crore was adjusted.  
An unspent balance of Rs. 26.00 lakhs has been allowed to be carried forward in 1999-2000 also.   The Committee
apprehends that the same situation may arise in 2000-2001 also.   The Committee takes serious view of such a trend
which is against all budgetary norms. The Department should take remedial measures in this regard without any further
delay.

93RD REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/93rdreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:11]
6.4       The Committee notes that the scope of Special Orientation Programme for School Teachers (SOPT) is being
widened to include secondary teachers.   The Committee finds that the  number of teachers trained under this
Programme during 1997-98 and 1998-99 shows drastic variations.   Out of 6,55,661 teachers trained,  3,39,643 teachers
were from the state of Maharashtra.   In contrast, in a state like Bihar, only 8,302 teachers were trained, and not a single
teacher was trained in Madhya Pradesh during this period.   The Committee is of the view that benefits  of such a
Training Programme should reach backward and tribal areas where literacy rate is still much below the average  literacy
rate of the country.   Efforts should be made to strengthen the existing structures of Teachers’ Training in such states. 
6.5       The Committee notes that a pilot project for in-service training of primary school teachers through inter-active
television has been taken up in the states of Gujarat and MP in collaboration with the Department of Telecom,
UNESCO and ITU under which 8000 teachers, teacher educators and educational supervisors are proposed to be
trained.
VII.      NON-FORMAL EDUCATION SCHEME
7.1       The Committee has been informed that the centrally sponsored scheme of Non-Formal Education has been
modified, keeping in view the various findings of the Planning  Commission  and feed-back from various studies and
also in keeping with the announcement  made by the Finance Minister in his Budget Speech to introduce Education
Guarantee scheme.    The revised scheme has since been approved by EFC and the process of obtaining Cabinet
approval is on.
7.2       The proposed scheme to be known as the ‘Scheme of Alternative and Innovative Education’ seeks to provide
primary education in a flexible manner at a convenient pace and location through locally recruited and trained
instructors.  Priority will be given to 10 educationally backward states.  It provides for :-
-           Demand driven establishment of EGS Learning Centres/alternative  Schools in unserved habitations.
-           Residential camps to prepare children for primary school through condensed and short time courses.
-           Remedial short term teaching programmes in urban slums
-           A flexible approach for adolescent girls to meet diversity of their learning needs.
-           Decentralisation to PRIs.
-           The Centre-State ratio for sharing of expenditure would be 75:25
-           The unit cost per child per annum revised from the present Rs. 375/-  to Rs. 845/- for an EGS Primary
Centre and from  Rs. 580/- to Rs. 1200/- for an upper primary centre.
7.3       The  Committee hopes that the revised scheme would be operationalised in 2000-2001 for which necessary
provision of Rs. 300 crore has been made.  The Committee also hopes that the scheme will be implemented smoothly
with proper coordination between Central Government, State Governments  and voluntary agencies.   In view of the
enhanced financial norms in the revised scheme, there is a need for having an effective inbuilt monitoring mechanism. 
The Committee is of the view that alongwith regular inspections, a component of random surveys without prior notice
should also be evolved to have proper assessment of the implementation of the revised scheme and  also elimination of
undesirable NGOs.
VIII.     NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT TO PRIMARY EDUCTION (MID-DAY
MEAL SCHEME)
8.1       The      programme launched on 15
th august, 1995,  is intended to give a boost to universalisation of primary
education while simultaneously catering to the nutritional needs of the students in primary classes.  During 1999-2000,
the estimated number of beneficiaries is 9.80 lakh children. The Committee was informed that the requirement of funds
for 2000-2001 will be Rs. 2300 crore in view of increase in the economic cost of foodgrains.   However, only Rs. 1090
crore have been provided which will need to be augmented at the RE stage.    The Committee observes that the position
was the same in 1998-99.
8.2       As per the guidelines, the distribution of foodgrains is an interim measure till arrangements are made by the
implementing agencies for providing hot cooked meal/ready to eat food.   Such arrangements were required to be
developed within a period of two years from the date of introduction of the programme.  At present, only the states/UT
of Gujarat, Kerala, Orissa, Tamil Nadu, Pondicherry and MP (174 Tribal Blocks) are providing cooked meals. 
8.3       The Committee was given to understand that paucity of funds is the main reason for not switching over to
cooked meals by the states/UTs.  It has been estimated that  in the Ninth Plan  alone, Rs. 18,000 crore would be required

to convert foodgrains into cooked meals as against a requirement of Rs. 12,615 crore towards cost and transportation of
foodgrains alone.   It is mainly due to this that   Haryana and J&K had to revert to  foodgrain distribution.
8.4       The Committee is constrained to note that out of an allocation of 27.07 lakh metric tonne  foodgrains, only 11.47
lakh metric tonne was lifted to cover 9.75 lakh children.  Non-receipt /non-reconciliation of lifting figures with FCI has
been cited as the main factor responsible for inadequate coverage of Mid day Meal Scheme.    The Committee finds that
Goa, Kerala, Orissa, Tripura , Chandigarh, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Pondicherry and MP are the states/UTs where
allocation has been made after deducting the unutilised balance.  The Committee is perturbed to note that the states/UTs
other than mentioned above, have not yet supplied enrolment data and/or unutilised quantity of foodgrains available
with them and therefore provisional allocation has been made to them.   The Committee is of the view that drastic
remedial measures are required in this direction.   The Committee feels that the expansion of serving of cooked meals 
under this scheme to all the states can perhaps never be implemented in view of the lack of initiative and non-adherence
to budgetary norms by majority of the states.   The Committee is of the  view that there is a need of  intervention at
higher level to tackle this problem.
8.5       The Committee  feels  that providing of foodgrains instead of cooked meals to the children does not serve any
purpose  and it also goes against the ultimate goal of the scheme.   The Committee therefore recommends that the matter
should be taken up at higher level with the states not serving cooked meals.
IX.       EXTERNALLY-AIDED PROJECTS DISTRICT PRIMARY EDUCATION PROGRAMME (DPEP)
9.1       The scheme launched in 1994 aims at operationalising holistic approach for achieving UEE in selected districts,
promoting decentralized planning and management with district as a unit.  The scheme is under implementation in 219
low female  Literacy districts  in 15 States.  The project is funded 85% by external agencies through the Central Budget
and the concerned  State Governments contribute 15% .   The Committee was given to understand that expansion of
DPEP in 41 additional districts of Uttar Pradesh, 10 districts of Rajasthan and 5 districts of West Bengal has since been
approved by the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC).  Appraisal of project plans for expansion of DPEP in  8
additional districts of Orissa has  been initiated.  Further expansion of DPEP in 9 additional districts of Rajasthan and 6
districts of Gujarat is also envisaged.        The Committee desires that, as proposed, the new centres would be started
early.
9.2       The Committee was informed that provision of Rs. 750 crore in BE 1999-2000 was reduced to Rs. 600 crore,
keeping in view the various factors , including the availability of funds with the State Implementation  Societies and the
trend of expenditure.  However, since the expenditure has picked up in the later part of the year, provision at final grant
stage was enhanced to Rs. 700 crore by re-appropriation.  The Committee observes that pace of expenditure has been
slower than anticipated in 1997-98 and 98-99 also as the State Implementation Societies were having unspent balances
from the previous year’s releases. 
9.3       Last year, the Committee had observed that certain problems were arising in the implementation of DPEP in
Kerala.  The Department has informed that a joint inquiry  had been initiated by the State Govt. of Kerala to review the 
work and progress and also  to inquire into the affairs of the DPEP in Kerala.  The problem was on the revised textbooks
specially Malayalam textbooks in classes I and II.  There was also some controversy about the new  pedagogical
methods in DPEP in the state.   Text books which raised controversy have been revised based on the interim  report of
the Guptan Nair Committee appointed by the Kerala Government.  It has also been informed that resistance of
parents/teachers to the pedagogical changes has now worn off. The Committee would appreciate if final
recommendation of the Guptan Nair Committee as and when received, are made known to it. 
9.4       The Committee expresses its concern over the State-wise expenditure details  under DPEP for the last three
years.  It is surprising that while no money was spent  in Rajasthan in 1997-98 & 1998-99, only Rs. 2.13 crores has been
shown in expenditure details as upto January, 2000.   In contrast, expenditure in  Madhya Pradesh is Rs. 392.32 crores
in the last three years.  Unspent balances lying with the states indicate that the scheme is not  being properly
implemented there. Therefore, proper monitoring of the scheme is urgently called for. The Committee notes that delay
in the release of 15% state share  stay  on recruitment of teachers due to court cases, frequent transfer of Project
Directors in some States have sometimes adversely affected the pace of programme implementation in the concerned
project States.  Steps need to be taken in these areas for effective implementation.

REPORT
I.          INTRODUCTION
1.1
              Education is the most crucial investment in human development.  It is an instrument for developing an
economically prosperous society and for ensuring equity and social justice.  With this realization, the importance of
Secondary Education which provides skilled manpower for the economy and is a bridge for higher, technical and
professional education cannot be denied.  With the process of liberalization and globalisation the economy generates
higher demand for new skills. In this context Higher Education and need for it is imperative.  A holistic view was taken
in 1986 when the National Policy on Education (NPE) visualized education as a dynamic, cumulative, life long process,
providing diversity of learning opportunities to all segments of society. Prime Minister’s Special Action Plan (SAP) has
also stressed the need for expansion and improvement of social infrastructure in the field of education.  With the 
necessity of qualitative skilled manpower,  a separate Department of Secondary Education and Higher Education has
been created recently.
1.2
              During the course of his evidence, Secretary, Department of Secondary and Higher Education  informed  the
Committee that an allocation of Rs. 24,908 crore has been made in the Ninth Five Year Plan in the Central Sector as
against an outlay of Rs. 7,443 crore in the Eighth Five Year Plan. While this represents an increase of more than two
and a half times, it is less than one third of the actual requirement projected.  During the first three years of the current
Five Year Plan, an expenditure of Rs. 11,951,03 crore is likely to be incurred (Approx. 48%).  An amount of Rs.
12,957.35 crore is expected to be available for allocation  during the last two years of the current Five Year Plan.  50%
of the amount i.e. Rs. 6,478.67 crore should have been allocated to the Department during 2000-2001.  Actual allocation
has been restricted to Rs. 5,450.00 crore, a shortfall of approximately, Rs. 1,000 crore.  Allocation for Secondary
Education & Higher Education is Rs.1720.29 crore as against Rs.1553.91 crore in 1999-2000 (BE) which shows an
increase of about 11%. However, the Committee was given to understand that even though several Committees have
suggested for 6% of GDP to be made available for Educational sector,  yet the present allocation is only 3.4% of GDP
which is still less by 2.6%.  The Committee in this respect is of the considered view that when there is a general trend
for disinvestment  of the  public sector and cuts in subsidies, it should be the effort  of the Government to prioritize the
Social Sector,  especially Education and Health which stand as the heart and soul of human development.   The
Committee, therefore,  suggests that the Department should find greater ways and means for  further development and
promotion of education.
II.         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       The Committee was informed that the allocation of Rs. 4786.37 crore for Secondary and Higher Education in BE
1999-2000  was reduced to Rs. 4380.80 crore at the RE stage.  Provision  for the same in BE 2000-2001  is Rs. 4650.38
crore which  is less when compared to the BE of previous year.
2.2       Allocation for Secondary Education is Rs. 600 crore as against Rs. 558.45 crore in 1999-2000 (BE), reflecting an
increase of about 7%.  Similarly, enhancement in allocation for Higher Education from Rs. 501.85 crore as against Rs.

445.94 crore provided in BE 1999-2000 shows an increase of about 13%.  Likewise, Technical Education has been
provided Rs. 500 crore as against an allocation of Rs. 452.18 crore in BE 1999-2000, showing an increase of about 11%.
2.3       The Committee observes that total allocation of Rs. 4786.37 crore in BE 1999-2000 had to be reduced to Rs.
4380.80 crore at the RE stage.  The Committee is constrained to note that the major reasons cited for reduction of
allocation in a number of schemes are unspent balance available with the States, low pace of expenditure, non-
performing NGOs, low absorption due to non-viable nature of the scheme and lack of quality proposals.  Allocation of
Rs. 4650.38 crore in BE 2000-2001 is at an enhanced level when compared to provision of Rs. 4380.80 crore in RE
1999-2000.  The Committee urges upon the Department to make concerted efforts to remove all the constraints which
led to reduction in the allocation of funds at the Re stage in 1999-2000 so as to ensure optimum and judicious utilisation
of funds provided for  secondary and higher education in 2000-2001.
2.4      Performance Budget should clearly reflect both the financial provision and corresponding physical achievements
of different schemes/programmes during the financial year.  The Committee, however, observes that Performance
Budgets of almost all the Departments are prepared in such a manner that one does not get a clear  idea in this regard. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take corrective steps in this regard, if the
Performance Budgeting is to have any meaning.
III.       SECONDARY EDUCATION
Against a provision of Rs. 558.45 crore in BE 1999-2000 for Secondary Education, allocation for 2000-2001
stands at Rs. 600 crore, thus reflecting a marginal increase.  The Committee, however, observes that trend of allocation
of funds and expenditure thereof during the period 1997-2000 clearly indicates that the funds provided were invariably
reduced at the RE stage and even the reduced allocation could not be fully utilised due to one reason or the other.  The
Committee feels that secondary education is a critical stage of education where the process of transformation from
childhood to adulthood occurs.  It can become gateway to higher education for the talented students and for others a
stage for entry into the world of work.  The Committee is,  therefore, of the view that special emphasis at this stage is 
called for.  The Department should actively monitor the successful implementation of the various schemes of the
secondary education sector.
IV.       NATIONAL COUNCIL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH AND TRAINING (NCERT)
4.1       NCERT is an apex resource organisation to assist and advise the Central and the State Governments on academic
matters related to school education.  It provides academic and technical support for qualitative improvement of school
education.  The Secretary informed the Committee that keeping in view the requirements of the National Education
Policy,  steps to review the 10 year old National curriculum framework have been initiated by the NCERT.  NCERT has
recently initiated a national debate on its document on “National Curriculum Framework for School Education”, where
the focus is on:-
i)
                    Work experience/life coping skill development;
ii)                   Value Education;
iii)                 Reduction in content/load and load of non-comprehension ;and
iv)                 Information Technology (IT) literacy and increasing use of IT in teaching and learning.
It was clarified by the Secretary that this document was a discussion document which has only mentioned the
issues being raised by many educationists/experts in various quarters.   This document was being debated at present.  It
was further clarified that there was no change in the National  Policy on medium of instruction and teaching of
languages in schools and the discussion document will be finalised in line with the national policy.  The Committee
feels that mother tongue should be taught right from the first standard. However, the Committee finds that in reality this
is not happening.   Most of the privately managed schools are not following the national policy in this regard.
4.2       The Committee has been informed that allocation for NCERT in BE 1999-2000 was Rs.34.70 crore which was
increased to Rs.40 crore at the RE stage and in BE 2000-2001 it has further been enhanced to Rs.43 crores.  The
Committee is, however, constrained to observe that the real increase is reflected  only in the non-plan allocation. 
Provision of Rs. 20.70 crore (Non-plan) in BE 1999-2000 was enhanced to Rs. 30 crore at the RE stage.  Same
allocation has been  made in BE 2000-2001.  In contrast,  plan allocation of Rs. 14 crore in BE 1999-2000 was reduced
to Rs. 10 crore at the RE stage.  Rs. 13 crore have been given in 2000-2001 which is less than  BE 1999-2000.  Reason
given for reduction is slow pace of expenditure.  The Committee desires that steps should be taken for the optimum and
judicious utilisation of plan funds meant for various schemes for qualitative improvement of school education.

V.        KENDRIYA VIDYALAYAS
5.1       The main objective of  Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan set up in 1965 is to provide uninterrupted educational
facilities  to the wards of Central Govt. employees who are transferred from one region to another and from one
linguistic area to another.  At present, there are 871 KVs in India including two abroad at Kathmandu and Moscow. 707
KVs are in Civil/Defence Sectors and the remaining 164 are Projects and Institutes of Higher learning.
5.2       Against an allocation of Rs. 544.81 crore in BE 1999-2000, an enhanced provision of Rs. 590.59 crore has been
made in 2000-2001.  Rs. 95 crore is the plan component and Rs. 495.59 crore have been provided under non-plan. 
Additional allocation is proposed to be utilised to meet the increased expenditure on maintenance and repairs of school
buildings affected by severe cyclone in Orissa and other routine expenditure.
5.3       The Committee finds that out of 707 KVs in Civil/Defence Sectors, at present 403 are in permanent buildings
and the construction work is in progress in respect of another 79 KVs.  In respect of 89 KVs, the land has been
transferred and work is to be started.  Out of the total Ninth Plan outlay of Rs. 553.21 crore in the first three years, an
allocation of Rs. 217.18 crore has been made.  A requirement of Rs. 168 crore for each year, i.e. 2000-2001 and 2001-
2002 has accordingly, been projected.  The Committee observes that out of a plan allocation of Rs. 90 crore in 1999-
2000, Rs. 68.80 crore were earmarked for construction of School Buildings and Staff Quarters.  The Committee is,
however, constrained to note that whereas non-plan provision of Rs. 454.81 crore has been fully utilised upto 29.2.2000,
against a plan allocation of Rs. 90 crore, expenditure reported upto 29.2.2000 is only Rs. 45 crore.  The Committee
apprehends that there are chances of funds not being fully utilised for construction activities.  The Committee observes
that the Department should take appropriate measures for removal of constraints if any, in this regard.  The Committee
also recommends that allocation may be enhanced at the RE stage on the condition that it must be ensured that targets
set for construction activities are achieved.   The Committee would also like to point out that the Plan Schemes are
being transferred to Non-Plan, thereby adjusting the amount of committed expenditure.  The Committee strongly objects
to this kind of adjustment.
5.4       The Committee would also like to point out that children of local people  should get admission in Kendriya
Vidyalayas and the Committee recommends accordingly.  The Department should report to the Committee about the
action taken in this regard.

IX.       INTEGRATED EDUCATION FOR DISABLED CHILDREN (IEDC)
9.1       IEDC is a centrally sponsored scheme launched in 1974 which aims at providing educational opportunities  to
disabled children in schools to facilitate their retention and ultimate integration in the general school system.   The
scheme is being implemented through State Governments and NGOs.  The Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection
of Rights and Full Participation) Act 1955 places a statutory responsibility on the Government to ensure that all disabled
children receive free education in an appropriate environment till the age of 18 years.
9.2       The scheme  is being implemented in 27 States/UTs.  It is currently estimated that more than 65,000 disabled
children have benefitted under the scheme.   However, the Committee is perturbed to note that figures regarding number
of beneficiaries have not been received from 13 States/UTs.   The Committee observes that participation of the states
also does not seem to be of uniform level.   While States like Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Karnataka, and Orissa
are the major beneficiaries during 1998-99 and 1999-2000, no funds/nominal funds have been allocated to Bihar, J&K 
Punjab and Arunachal Pradesh.  The Committee is of the view that monitoring mechanism of this scheme should be
strengthened.   Matter should also be taken up with the states who have failed to furnish the details about beneficiaries.  
The Committee notes that NCERT  has been requested to conduct an impact study with a view to  ascertaining the
impact of the IEDC Scheme.

REPORT
I.          INTRODUCTION
            The development of women and children to their full potential is an essential component in the country’s total
human resource development.  In its  capacity as a nodal agency looking after the advancement of women and children,
the Department of Women & Child Development  formulates plans, policies and programmes, enacts/amends legislation
affecting women and children and guides and coordinates the efforts of both Governmental and non-Governmental
organisations working in the field of Women and Child Development.   Apart from this, the Department also
implements certain innovative programmes for women and children in the areas of employment and income generation,
welfare and support services, gender sensitization, training for employment and income generation and awareness
generation.   For a holistic child development, the Department implements the Integrated Child Development Services
(ICDS) which provides an integrated package of services comprising supplementary nutrition, immunisation, health 
check-up and pre-school and non-formal education and health and nutrition education.  The ultimate objective of all
these programmes is to make women independent and self-reliant and to ensure that children grow and live in a healthy
and secure environment.
II.         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       Total outlay for the Department for the 9
th Plan (1997-2000) is Rs. 7810.42 crores.   In the first three years of the
9th Plan, Rs. 4736.36 crores have been allocated and the remaining amount of Rs. 3074.06 crores is meant for 2000-
2001 and 2001-2002.   Plan allocation for 2000-2001 is Rs. 1460.00 crores which shows an enhancement of Rs. 140.00
crores when compared to Rs. 1320.00 crores provided in BE 1999-2000.  The Committee was given to understand that
this increase does not match the projected demand of the Department which was Rs. 2030.14 crores.  Higher outlays
were proposed for ICDS, World Bank Assisted ICDS, Mahila Samriddhi Yojana (MSY), Rashtriya Mahila Kosh
(RMK) and National Commission for Women.
2.2       The Committee finds that during 1998-99, the actual expenditure was Rs.1176.80 crores (Rs.1131.84 crores
under Plan and Rs. 44.96 crores under Non-Plan), against the BE provision of Rs. 1274.23 crores  (Rs.1225.95 crores
Plan and Rs. 48.28 crores Non-Plan) reduced to Rs. 1179.93crores (Rs. 1134.48 crores Plan and Rs. 45.45 crore  Non-
Plan) at the RE stage.
2.3       The Department’s annual outlay for 1999-2000 was Rs. 1371.83 crores (Rs.1320.00 crores Plan and Rs. 51.83
crores Non-Plan) which was reduced to the level of Rs. 1298.07 crores (Rs.1249.86 crores Plan + Rs. 48.21 crores Non
Plan) at the RE stage.   The Committee notes that the expenditure  reported upto 31
st January, 2000, is only Rs. 998.34
crores.
2.4       The Committee is constrained to note that allocation for schemes meant for women welfare has shown a
declining trend since 1998-99 and even this reduced allocation shows marked under-utilisation of funds as revealed
below:-

2.5       Allocation for schemes meant for women welfare has been further reduced to Rs. 150.88 crores in 2000-2001. 
Another disturbing feature is the trend of expenditure  during 1998-99 which reveals the maximum level in the month of
March (against a total plan expenditure of Rs. 1131.84 crores, figures for March stand at Rs. 474.52 crores). The
Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that there is a need for maximum and judicious expenditure of funds allocated

2.6       Performance Budget should clearly reflect both the financial provision and corresponding physical achievements
of different schemes/programmes during the financial year. The Committee, however, observes that Performance
Budgets of almost all the Departments are prepared in such a manner that one does not get a clear idea in this regard. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take corrective steps in this regard, if the
Performance Budgeting is to have any meaning.
III.       INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS) SCHEME
3.1       The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) Scheme implemented through State Govts./UT
Administrations, aims at providing an integrated package of services to the children below 6 years, pregnant women and
nursing mothers.  The services include supplementary nutrition, immunisation, health check-up, referral services, pre-
school and non-formal education and health and nutrition education.  The Scheme is at present operational in 4200
development blocks in the country. 
3.2       The Committee was informed that the proposed enhanced estimate of Rs. 935.00 crores in 2000-2001 is mainly
due to revised financial norms and proposed expansion of the scheme in additional 260 Blocks in the country. 
However, an additional amount of Rs. 264.00 crores was required to meet the full requirement.  The Committee is
happy to note that the revised cost norms of ICDS from Rs. 17.06 lakh to Rs. 30.75 lakh per project which relates to
costs of salaries of project staff, contingency amounts, provision of medicine  etc.  approved by the Govt. of India in
January, 2000, would be made effective in due course.   A noteworthy feature in the revised ICDS scheme is the
proposal to cover the small hamlets/villages in the country in tribal blocks  having less than 300 population and situated
in far flung areas.  It is now proposed that 10 Mini Anganwadi centres can be opened in lieu of a full-fledged
Anganwadi.
3.3       The main objective of ICDS is to improve nutritional and health status of children 0-6 years old.   This scheme
covers a major part of the country and there has been continued enhanced allocation and expenditure under it.  However,
the Committee is disturbed to note that this significant expansion of ICDS has not been able to reduce the Infant
Mortality Rate (IMR).  Figures for 1998 indicate no improvement and in case of some states there is  an increase in IMR
which  is a matter of great concern.  Figures for  the period 1996-98  in respect of weak states are self-revealing :-
 
State 1996 1997 1998
MP 97 94 97
Orissa 96 96 98
Uttar Pradesh 85 85 85
All India 72 71 72
 
3.4       Another disturbing element is the incidence of malnutrition deaths in tribal areas of the country.   The
Committee had drawn the attention of the Department in this regard last year too.  The Committee was informed that the

95th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/95threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:12]
State Govt. of Orissa has initiated mapping exercise so as to concentrate on pockets having high incidents of
malnutrition.  State Govts. of Madhya  Pradesh and Maharashtra have also prepared plans of action in collaboration with
the concerned Departments.  The Committee was also  informed that the Central Planning Committee has been regularly
holding meetings with representatives of State Govts. and concerned Central Ministries/Departments for monitoring
deaths of children due to  starvation/malnutrition in remote and tribal areas.  But holding of regular meetings does not
seem to be achieving any  results.   The Committee is not prepared to believe that the sudden spurt of death of children
in tribal areas occurs with the onset of monsoon in most of the cases.  The Committee is of the view that a specific Plan
of Action for such tribal areas may be prepared. The Committee finds that there is no dearth of
schemes/funds/implementing agencies, what is lacking is initiative and co-ordinated approach to tackle this problem.  
Department’s role does not  end with conveying its feeling of concern to the State Govts.  Instead of calling for reports
from the State Govts.,  fact-finding teams should be sent by the Department at regular intervals.  What is required is a
co-ordinated approach amongst all the concerned Central Departments and the State Govts. Initiative by the Department
of Women & Child Development in active cooperation from rest of the Departments can achieve results.            
3.5       The Committee was informed that as on 30.9.99, 3,70,908 Anganwadis were providing supplementary nutrition
to 257.88 lakh children and 51.61 lakh mothers and pre-school education was available to 126.95 lakh children.    
Nutrition supplement is the responsibility of the State Govts. which varies from State to State as per the local
requirements.   External  agencies like CARE and World Food Programme were providing  assistance to some of the
States.  However,  the Committee was given to understand that due to resource constraint, some State Govts. were not in
a position to fulfil this responsibility as per the prescribed norms.  The Committee is of the view that the Department
should prevail upon the State Governments to ensure that provision of nutrition-cum-supplement should not be
adversely affected due to lack of funds.  Steps may be taken for provision of assistance from external agencies to the
extent possible to such States.
3.6       The Committee would like to draw the attention of the Department to instances of nutritious supplement not
reaching the beneficiaries due to one reason or the other.   Anganwadi Workers find it difficult to collect the nutritious
supplement from CDPO office in the absence of any transport charges being given to them.  The Committee urges upon
the Department to look into the matter and take necessary remedial measures.
3.7       The effective delivery package of services envisaged in the ICDS scheme depends upon the functioning of
Anganwadi Worker, who is a community-based voluntary worker and her helper.  Feedback made available to the
Committee indicates that successful running of an Anganwadi centre, by and large, depends upon the initiative and
dedication of an individual Anganwadi worker. However, the Committee finds that as compared to her manifold duties,
honorarium paid to an Anganwadi Worker is too meagre.  The Committee was given to understand that an Anganwadi
Worker is a part-time worker, but ground realities are totally different.  There is large scale exploitation of Anganwadi
Workers in most of the States.   Anganwadi Workers, generally being uneducated are neither aware nor properly briefed
about the various services available for child/women welfare. 
3.8       The Committee  was informed that 14 States, where additional work was being done by Anganwadi Workers
and Helpers, have started giving additional remuneration ranging from Rs. 100 to Rs. 250 to as high as Rs. 650 in the
case of Pondicherry.   Three more States are likely to provide additional remunerations.  The Committee is of the view
that honorarium of Rs. 500 for AWW and Rs. 200 for Helper needs to be increased in the present scenario.  Lack of
resources cannot be held responsible for it.  It is for the Department to manage funds by streamlining the existing
schemes. 
3.9       The Committee finds that the report of the National Committee to review the benefits/facilities to AWWs and
Helpers is under finalisation and hopes that the implementation of the recommendations made by the aforesaid
Committee would lead to a significant improvement in the service conditions of AWWs and Helpers.  The Committee
would like to be apprised in this regard.
3.10     The Committee finds that there are Central directives for running of Anganwadi centres but the implementation
thereof  varies from State to State.  The Committee notes that as per the central directives, there has to be a local
committee for selection of Anganwadi Workers and it is for State Governments to decide the composition of the
Committee.  The Department submitted that the mode of involvement of PRIs in implementation of ICDS scheme
differs from State to State depending on the powers conferred upon them by the State Govts.   The Committee was
given to understand that in States where Panchayati Raj Institutions are traditionally strong like MP, AP, West Bengal,
UP, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Kerala etc., the supervision and management of the Anganwadi centres is actively done

through Panchayats.  However, in some of the States where Panchayat elections have not been held for long, like Bihar,
involvement of PRIs is weak.   The Committee is of the opinion that there should be a uniform pattern for running of
Anganwadi centres through PRIs/local bodies.    The Committee feels that selection criteria for AWWs should also be
uniform and fool-proof.  Specific guidelines both for selection of AWWs and running of  Anganwadi centres should be
framed and States should be prevailed  upon to implement the same in the real sense.  The Committee feels that  if
urgent steps are not taken in this direction, then element of favouritism and resultant exploitation of AWWs which
defeats the very purpose of ICDS scheme would continue.
3.11     The Committee hopes that the National Evaluation of ICDS being conducted by NCAER, likely to be concluded
shortly, would give a proper analysis of State-wise performance of ICDS. The Committee, however, observes that there
is a need for having a  strong in-built system of monitoring for ICDS.
IV.       WORLD BANK ASSISTED ICDS
4.1       The Committee notes that at present three on-going World Bank assisted ICDS Projects are there:
i)          ICDS-II Project in Bihar and MP (1993-2000)
ii)         ICDS-III in Kerala, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu and UP (1999-2004)
iii)         ICDS-APER – AP (1999-2004)
The  World Bank assisted ICDS-II Project  in Bihar and Madhya Pradesh became operational in September,
1993 for a period of seven years.   The Project covers 210 blocks in Bihar and 244 blocks in Madhya Pradesh in
predominantly tribal and difficult areas.   The total outlay for the Project, excluding the cost of Supplementary Nutrition
Programme is Rs. 596.23 crores – Rs. 257.13 crores for Bihar and Rs. 339.10 crores for Madhya Pradesh. 
4.2       The World Bank Assisted ICDS-III Project has been in operation  in five States of Kerala, Maharashtra,
Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh since March, 1999.  The approved IDA credit available for the ICDS-III
Project, including the UDISHA  Project is, US$ 300 million.  The total outlay for the Project is Rs. 1000.11 crores over
a five year Project period from 1998-99 to 2003-2004 (excluding the training component).  An amount of Rs. 75.90
crores has been released to the five States so far for implementation of the project.
4.3       Andhra Pradesh Economic Restructuring (APER) Project is being implemented in the State of Andhra Pradesh
since March, 1999.   The approved IDA Credit for the Project is US$ 75 million.   The Project would be covering a total
of 251 blocks at a project cost of Rs. 392.75 crores .
4.4       The Committee was informed that the additional components under World Bank assisted ICDS Projects are
construction of Anganwadi centres, construction of CDPOs Office-cum-Godowns, installation of hand pumps, enhanced
Information,  Education and Communication activities, provision of micro-nutrients for adolescent girls.  The
Committee was informed that as against proposed outlay of Rs. 293.81 crores,  Rs. 180.00 crores have been provided
for the year 2000-2001.
4.5       The Committee notes that so far Rs. 270.80  crores and Rs. 280.80 crores have been released to Bihar and
Madhya Pradesh (December, 1999) respectively under ICDS-II project.  The Committee has been given to understand
that despite a slow start, the project has picked up very well in both States.   Comparison of the National Family Health
Survey (1992-93) data with NFHS (1999) and India Nutrition Profile  (1998) data indicates that there has been
improvement in Bihar in growth and survival indicators over the life of the project.   However, the Committee has an
apprehension that ground realities may be somewhat different.   The Committee feels that an in-depth evaluation by an
independent agency with active interaction with field workers and beneficiaries and involvement of Panchayats/local
bodies and also with local MPs/MLAs wherever feasible in the most vulnerable areas (particularly in tribal and remote
areas) would give the real assessment of this Project.

9.1       The Scheme of Balika Samriddhi Yojana was launched on 2 nd October, 1997 with the objective of raising the
overall status of the girl child.  Re-designed in 1999-2000, the post-delivery grant of Rs. 500/- will now be deposited in
an interest-bearing bank/post office account in the name of the girl child  and a scholarship ranging from Rs. 300 to Rs.
1000 for each class of study successfully completed upto Class X. ICDS/Village Panchayats/Municipalities are the
actual implementing agencies
9.2       The Committee is perturbed to note that the releases made under the scheme in 1997-98 and 1998-99 totalled to

flaw in the scheme itself.  The Committee feels   that submission of utilisation certificates of releases already made
should be a mandatory pre-condition for future releases. The Committee would also like to point that at present adequate
publicity of such schemes beneficial for girl child is lacking at the grass-root level.  Panchayats/Anganwadi Workers
need to be fully acquainted of benefits of such schemes so as to reach the remotest corners of the country.   The
Committee is of the view that subject to resource-availability, possibility of giving some extra incentives under this
scheme to families adopting small family norms may be explored.
X.        WORKING WOMEN’S HOSTELS
10.1     The objective of the scheme is to provide cheap and safe hostel accommodation to employed women living out
of their homes.  The targetted beneficiaries  are single working women, widows, divorcees etc.
10.2     The Committee is happy to note that as recommended by it, women getting training for employment and girl
students studying in post school professional courses have also become eligible to stay in the hostels.  The Committee
would, however, like to  point out that pace of construction of hostels has been rather slow.  The Committee finds that
since the inception of the scheme in 1972-73, out of 873 hostels sanctioned, only 599 hostels have been completed so
far.  Out of these 599   completed  hostels too, 194 hostels could not be completed within the prescribed time limit of 2
years of their sanction.    The Committee hopes that the specific measures taken by the Department by actively
coordinating with the NGOs/State Govts. would yield the desired results.   The Committee would like to have the
details  of  functional hostels.

11.1     Under this Scheme, grants-in-aid are given to voluntary organisations for establishing and running Short Stay
Homes for rehabilitating women and girls, facing social and moral danger.
11.2     The Committee notes that against an allocation of Rs. 13.52 crores in 1999-2000 reduced to Rs. 8.51 crores at
the RE stage, expenditure of Rs. 6.76 crores has been incurred upto 31.1.2000.   The Committee has been informed that
in 1997-98 and 1998-99, the actual expenditure was less than revised estimates on account of lower releases to NGOs
due to unspent balances available with them.  Moreover, it was considered necessary that new Homes may not be
opened until the scheme is revised.  The Committee notes that as per the revised norms, recently approved by CCEA,
the recurring cost will now be Rs. 4,01,350 per Home per annum in ‘C’ class city with a  one time non-recurring cost of
Rs.50,000. The Committee hopes that the implementation of the scheme being transferred to CSWB and introduction of
the system of pre-sanction appraisal of proposals submitted by NGOs would lead to better performance of NGOs and
elimination of unhealthy trend of unspent balances lying with them.  The Committee would reiterate that system of both
regular and surprise inspections followed up by required  corrective measures should continue. The Committee would
also recommend that surprise inspection of SSHs should also be  carried out by CSWB directly on a sample basis. The
Committee hopes that as recommended earlier, CSWB would initiate attempts to rehabilitate the inmates of Short Stay
Homes on a regular basis.

XX.      COMMITTED LIABILITY
20.1     The issue of Committed Liability has been engaging the attention of the Committee since 1997-98.  At the end
of the Eight Five Year Plan, the Planning Commission had issued very detailed guidelines to carry forward the
Committed Expenditure from Plan to the Non-Plan side.  A lump sum provision of Rs. 500 crores in the Ministry of
Finance Budget for 1997-98 was provided for this purpose.  As a result of this exercise, however, only a sum of Rs. 150
crores was  transferred from Plan to Non-Plan for the various Ministries as committed expenditure during 1997-98. 
Rest of the amount was surrendered as the proposals were not found acceptable.  Secretary (Expenditure) while
deposing before the Committee on 27
th March, 1999 had informed that the Tenth Finance Commission had given a
breathing time till 1999-2000 for this transition.
20.2     The Department has informed that a proposal to transfer committed expenditure from Plan to Non-Plan for the
amount of Rs. 2.75 crores under the scheme of Short Stay Homes was submitted  to the Ministry of Finance in
November, 1997.  The proposal was revised in 1999-2000 due to revision of norms of the  scheme and the matter has
been pursued with that Ministry during 1999-2000.  The Ministry of Finance (Budget Division) has informed that the
matter will be considered during pre-Budget discussions while deciding the RE for 1999-2000.
20.3     The Committee notes with serious concern that while grants for Plan Schemes are getting reduced, Non-Plan
allocation and expenditure are steadily increasing.   What is happening is that the committed expenditure which should
appropriately be charged to the Pool, is being passed on to the respective Departments which is totally against the
guidelines of Tenth Finance Commission/Planning Commission.  If the committed expenditure is charged to the Pool, it
will not have any burden on the specific schemes of the Department.  Secretary (Expenditure), who appeared before the
Committee last year, was in full agreement with the stand taken by the Committee.   The Committee  is, however,
constrained to observe that in spite of Committee’s repeated efforts/directives to assist the Departments, no progress has
been made in the matter.   It seems that breathing time till 1999-2000 given by  the Tenth Finance Commission has not
been availed of by any Department.    There is total lack of initiative on the part of the Departments.  The Committee
again emphasises  that the Department should get this matter resolved without any further delay.   The way the 
Department including Ministry of Finance is trying to escape their responsibility is against the expressed wishes of the
Finance Commission and the recommendations made by the Committee.  This tendency, the Committee is constrained
to observe, is not in consonance with the principles which are well-established.   The Committee again reiterates that the
Department should pursue the matter and report to the Committee about the outcome thereof.
XXI.    GENERAL
21.1     The Committee had observed last year that several training and employment programmes of women of weaker
sections of society were being run by the Department, having identical components and same implementing agencies,
which was leading to all kinds of problems and ultimately  indirectly negating the very objective of the scheme.   The
Committee had, accordingly, recommended that there was a  need for convergence of all such schemes under one
umbrella scheme.  The Committee notes that the Department has initiated an exercise of having an umbrella scheme for
micro-enterprise development for women by merging the following schemes:-
i)          Scheme for setting up of Employment and income generation units for women  (NORAD)
ii)         Support to Training and Employment Programme for Women (STEP)
iii)         Condensed Courses of Education and Vocational Training Programme (CCE & VT); and
iv)        Socio-Economic Programme (SEP)
            The Committee, however, would like to point out that efforts should be made to put this initiative into effect
without any undue delay.
21.2     A ‘National Evaluation and Monitoring Agency’ was proposed to be launched during 1999-2000 for proper
identification of NGOs involved in various schemes of women and child development and also for evaluating and
monitoring the implementation of various schemes.   The Committee however, finds that this idea is not being pursued 
now.  Instead the Committee has been given to understand that  this component has been  incorporated in the proposed
revised Research, Publications  and Monitoring Scheme. However, the Committee observes that under this scheme,
Research Institutes/Universities/Voluntary  Organisations etc. are assisted to undertake research/evaluation studies and

also for organisation of seminars/workshops for capacity-building for monitoring activities.   The Committee feels that
monitoring is a very small  component in the scheme. The Committee expresses its serious concern over element of
uncertainty  in respect of such a vital issue. The Committee finds that majority of the schemes are being implemented by

system of regular review of all  the schemes for weeding out the flaws/weaknesses of a particular scheme.   The
Department needs to take a decision in this regard at the earliest.
21.3     The Committee is of the opinion  that there is general lack of awareness about the various schemes being run for
the welfare of both children and women.   Modalities of administering a particular scheme and its resultant benefits
should be known to the grass-root level  workers.   Otherwise these schemes would simply remain on paper.   The
Department should take specific measures in this regard. As per the feedback made available to the committee,
Anganwadi Workers face a number of difficulties in interacting with BDOs and other concerned local officials.   The
Committee is of the opinion that awareness-generation in respect of all the schemes should be a component of Training
Programme for ICDS functionaries, specially Anganwadi Workers and Helpers.  Efforts should also be made to
streamline the procedural aspects of all the schemes so as to make it more practical and easier for grass-root level
workers. IEC activities also need strengthening for this purpose.   The Committee is of the view that the Department 
should make special efforts for targeting the remote and tribal areas so that they do not  remain outside the purview of
such laudable schemes.

          The Committee notes with concern that some Departments are not furnishing the required information/papers
